newsitem.title: FRANCE: French firms unclear on capital gains tax.
newsitem.headline: French firms unclear on capital gains tax.

text.p: France's finance ministry said companies will have to wait until the autumn to find out exactly which corporate holdings are excluded from a rise in corporate capital gains tax announced this week.
"Companies aren't certain what to think because the distinction between company stakes and company investments is not clear," said Martine Leonard, responsible for financial analysis at CIC.
Officials at the finance ministry said there was margin for interpretation and it would be necessary to wait until the autumn when the measures will be put into law to know more.

"People will have to wait for the vote on the text (of the law) and the decrees to implement it," said a ministry spokesman. "The tax legislation service is preparing the instructions and this will be ready in September."

The government announced on Monday that taxes on capital gains by companies with more than 50 million francs in turnover would jump to 41.6 percent from 19 percent. The measure, aimed at bringing down France's deficit to qualify for European monetary union, would bring in six billion francs in 1997.
It is supposed to affect only capital gains from financial investments and not from gains on disposal of corporate stakes, said the finance ministry.

In 1995, the ministry defined a corporate stake as "one in which long-term ownership is believed useful to the company's activities, notably because it allows the exercise of influence on the company issuing the shares or to hold control".

The ministry rule specified that excluded from this definition were "stakes acquired in the pursuit of financial short-term gain" and that "the long-term durable nature of ownership...is a necessary condition for the qualification of these stakes but not sufficient."

The ministry said criteria for defining whether holding the shares in the company was useful to that firm included industrial synergies, diversification strategy or the control the stake allows the holder to exercise on the company.
The ministry spokesman said whether a holding met such criteria was done on a case by case basis by the courts.
For financial analysts and a number of firms, uncertainties remain over which holdings the tax hikes would affect. This, in turn, makes it difficult to calculate profits.

"The government must clarify things because it's easy for companies to say that these are strategic holdings," CIC's Leonard said. "There is room for interpretation and the companies we are contacting are very cautious," she said.
